title: Many forces at once
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 5 Physics (friction, air resistance, water resistance, upthrust, multiple forces). No textbook needed.
summary: A skydiver can fall at 200 kilometres an hour with the forces on her balanced. Balanced forces do not mean stopped: they mean no change in speed or direction. Your child draws force diagrams, adds forces to predict how things will move, and tests the forces that push back on moving things: air resistance and water resistance. They make parachutes, race clay shapes through water and build a balloon rocket.
builds_on: Class 1: pushes and pulls. Class 2: forces change speed, direction and shape. Class 3: measuring forces in newtons, and friction. Class 4: balance points, levers, pressure, upthrust and floating. This year puts them together: many forces on one thing at once. Gravity has its own topic this year too.
subconcepts: several forces act on everything at once
force diagrams: one labelled arrow for each force
adding forces in a line: the resultant force
balanced forces: no change in speed or direction, even when moving fast
unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or turning
friction holds still things still, up to a limit
air resistance grows with speed and with a bigger front
parachutes: a big area for a slow, safe fall
terminal speed: when air resistance grows to equal weight
every force has a partner: push something and it pushes you back
rockets push out gas, so they work in space
fair tests with repeats, the middle value, tables and graphs
goals: By the end your child can draw a force diagram with labelled arrows (gravity, upthrust, friction, air resistance, push or pull) for an object.
By the end your child can add forces in a line to find the overall (resultant) force, and say whether the object will speed up, slow down or keep the same speed.
By the end your child can explain air resistance and water resistance as kinds of friction that grow when things move faster or have a bigger front.
By the end your child can plan and carry out a fair test with repeats, present results in a table and a graph, and draw a conclusion.
By the end your child can explain why a parachute falls slowly and why a skydiver reaches a steady speed.
words: the overall force when all the forces on something are added up
forces that cancel out, so speed and direction stay the same
forces that don't cancel, so the object speeds up, slows down or turns
the push of air against something moving through it
the push of water against something moving through it
shaped to move through air or water with little resistance
the upward push of a liquid or gas
a drawing with arrows showing every force on an object
the steady top speed of a falling object when air resistance equals its weight

days.title: Every force on one thing
days.goal: Draw force diagrams for everyday objects.

steps.title: Remember Class 4
steps.do: Start by remembering last year. Ask: 'Why did the steel katori float but the iron nail sink?' (The katori pushes aside more water, so the upthrust is big enough to hold it up.) 'Why is a bottle with sand at the bottom hard to topple?' (Its centre of mass is low.) Then ask: 'Which forces are acting on you right now, as you sit?' (Gravity pulls you down. The chair pushes you up.) Say: 'Today we draw every force on one thing at once.'

steps.title: Force diagram gallery
steps.do: Draw force diagrams together for: a book on a table (gravity down, table push up), a floating boat (gravity down, upthrust up), a cycle moving at steady speed (pedal push forward, friction and air resistance back, gravity down, road push up), a falling leaf (gravity down, air resistance up). Rules: one arrow per force, starting on the object, pointing the way the force acts, longer for bigger, and labelled. Use Worksheet ws1.

steps.title: Add them up
steps.do: Use numbers. Write: 'A box is pushed right with 10 N. Friction pushes left with 4 N. What's the overall force?' (6 N to the right, so it speeds up to the right.) Then: 'Push 5 N right, friction 5 N left?' (0 N: balanced. If it was moving, it keeps the same speed. If still, it stays still.) Do three more with your child making up the numbers.

days.title: Tug of war maths
days.goal: Find the resultant of several forces with the forcemeter and with people.

steps.title: Three-way tug
steps.do: Two people pull a dupatta one way and one person the other. Ask before you start: 'Who'll win? Why?' Then try. Ask: 'What would make it a draw?'

steps.title: Forcemeter tug of war
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: hook two forcemeters to a box, one on each side, and pull. Use the rubber-band forcemeters from Class 3, or two spring balances from a hardware shop. Before each pull, ask: 'Which way will the box move?'

steps.title: Force Duel
steps.do: Play the Force Duel card game (g1). Each turn adds or subtracts forces on a cart. Players race to work out the resultant and the cart's motion.

need: two forcemeters or rubber bands with rulers

days.title: Air resistance
days.goal: Feel and test the push of air.

steps.title: Paper race
steps.do: Drop a flat sheet of paper and a scrunched ball of the same paper. Ask: 'Same paper, same weight. Why did the ball win?' (Less air pushing against it.)

steps.title: Parachute test
steps.do: Do Experiment e2: make parachutes with canopies of three sizes and time the fall from the same height, three times each.

steps.title: The first parachutes
steps.do: Talk about the first challenge question: did Faust Vrančić really jump from a tower in Venice with a parachute in 1617? Then discuss: 'How does a parachute change the forces on a person?' Draw it: gravity down, a big air-resistance arrow up.

need: a plastic bag or tissue paper
a small toy or a lump of clay as the load
a safe high place: an adult standing on a steady chair, or the top of a staircase

days.title: Graphs and the falling skydiver
days.goal: Turn results into a graph, and explain terminal speed.

steps.title: What does the table say?
steps.do: Look at the parachute table from Day 3. Ask: 'Which canopy fell slowest? Were the three times the same?' Choose the middle (median) time for each.

steps.title: Draw the graph
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2: draw a bar chart of canopy size against fall time, and write a conclusion: 'The bigger the canopy, the ___ the fall, because ___.'

steps.title: The skydiver story
steps.do: Tell your child what happens to a skydiver, and draw it together in four frames. (1) She jumps: only gravity, so she speeds up. (2) Faster: air resistance grows, she still speeds up but less. (3) Air resistance equals gravity: balanced forces, steady speed of about 200 km/h (terminal speed). (4) Parachute opens: a huge air resistance, unbalanced upwards, she slows down until a new, slow steady speed. Ask: 'In frame 3 she's falling fast. Are the forces balanced?' (Yes! Balanced means steady speed, not stopped.)

steps.title: Fix the mistake
steps.do: Say: 'My friend says if forces are balanced, a thing must be still.' Ask your child to correct the friend using the skydiver or a cycle at steady speed.

days.title: Water resistance and streamlining
days.goal: Test which shapes move through water fastest.

steps.title: Walk through water
steps.do: Fill a bucket with water. Your child moves a flat, open hand through the water, palm first, then turns the hand on its edge and moves it again. Ask: 'Which was harder? Why?' (The flat hand has a bigger front pushing against the water.)

steps.title: Shape race
steps.do: Do Experiment e3: drop two clay shapes of the same weight into a tall bottle of water at the same moment, and see which reaches the bottom first.

steps.title: Nature's shapes
steps.do: Ask: 'What shape do a fish, a dolphin and a diving kingfisher share?' (A pointed front, smooth sides, thin at the back.) Say: 'A shape like that is called streamlined. It moves through water or air with little resistance.' Then talk about voice v1: how an engineer in Japan copied the kingfisher's beak for a fast train. Ask the voice's question.

need: a tall clear bottle filled with water (or a long glass)
a spoon to fish shapes out

days.title: Rockets: action and reaction
days.goal: Build a balloon rocket and use forces to explain it.

steps.title: Push the wall
steps.do: Your child stands in socks on a smooth floor, facing a wall, with an adult behind them. They push the wall with both hands. Ask: 'What happened to you?' (They slid backwards.) 'You pushed the wall. What pushed you?' (The wall pushed back.) Say: 'Every push has a partner push, the same size, going the other way.'

steps.title: Story: The Rocket at Thumba
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'Why did the kattumaram slide backwards when Jose jumped?' and 'What did the rocket push against, high up where there is almost no air?' Accept any answers now. The balloon rocket will test them.

steps.title: Project: balloon rocket
steps.do: Do the project: build a balloon rocket on a string and improve it for distance.

steps.title: Rockets can't work in space?
steps.do: Talk about voice v2: in 1920 a newspaper said Robert Goddard's rockets could never work in space, because there is no air to push against. Ask the voice's question. Then read the perspective on Tipu Sultan's rockets from Mysuru and ask its question.

days.title: Review and teach it back
days.goal: Use all the forces from five years together.

steps.title: Challenge sheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. Encourage drawing a force diagram for every question.

steps.title: Big questions
steps.do: Talk about two big questions: 'If you threw a ball in deep space, far from everything, would it ever stop?' (No: there's no friction or air, so nothing slows it.) 'Why do cyclists crouch low in races?' (Less air resistance.)

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches the family 'Forces from Class 1 to Class 5' in five minutes, with one demonstration for each class: a push and a pull, a squashed ball of clay, the rubber-band forcemeter, the floating katori, and this year's balloon rocket. Then ask the check questions.

opts: keep moving at the same speed

A cycle rolls along a flat road at a steady speed. Shruti says no forces are acting on it. What would you tell her? Name the forces.
Fall times (seconds).
Draw a bar chart: canopy size along the bottom, middle fall time up the side.

The bigger the canopy, the ____ the fall, because ____.

A parachute with a toy falls at a slow, steady speed. Show the two forces on it.
Meera says that a parachute with a heavier load falls faster. Plan a test to find out. What will you change, what will you keep the same, and what will you measure?

worksheets.title: Forces puzzles
sections: A. Explain with a force diagram

sections.p: A skydiver falls at a steady 200 km/h. Are the forces on her balanced? Explain.
Why do fighter jets have pointed noses but parachutes are wide?

Divya says a rocket cannot work in space, because there is no air for it to push against. Her friend Zoya says it can. Who is right? Explain using your balloon rocket. Then say why Divya's idea seemed sensible.
Design a test to find out whether the shape of a paper boat changes how fast it can be pulled through water. What will you change, keep the same and measure?
A balloon rocket speeds to the right along a string. Show the forces along the string.
sections.obj: a balloon rocket on a string
options: air rushing out pushes balloon forward

a.name: air rushing out pushes balloon forward

sections.p: You flick a carrom striker. It slides across the board and slowly stops. What stops it?
opts: friction with the board, and air resistance

sections.p: Lakshmi pushes a heavy steel almirah with 50 N, and it does not move. How big is the friction on the almirah?
Farhan jumps from a small boat onto the shore, and the boat moves backwards. Explain why, using partner forces.

experiments.title: Forcemeter tug of war
experiments.question: How do two pulls add up?
need: two forcemeters: the rubber-band ones from Class 3, or two spring balances
a light box, such as an empty shoebox, on a smooth floor
steps: Hook one forcemeter to each side of the box.
Pull both with the same force (say 3 N each). Does it move?
Pull one side with 5 N and the other with 3 N. Which way does it move?
Write each pair and the resultant (bigger minus smaller, in the direction of the bigger).
experiments.predict: Before each, ask which way the box will move.
experiments.observe: The readings and the box's movement.
experiments.why: Forces in opposite directions take away from each other. If the two pulls are equal, the resultant is zero and the box stays still. If not, the box moves towards the bigger pull. Friction with the floor also acts against the movement, which is why a small difference may not move the box at all.

experiments.title: Parachute test
experiments.question: Does a bigger canopy make a parachute fall more slowly?
need: the same small load for each
a safe high place: an adult on a steady chair
steps: Cut three square canopies: 15 cm, 25 cm and 35 cm.
Tie a 25 cm thread to each corner and tie the four threads to the same load.
Drop each one from the same height, about 2 metres, holding it the same way: an adult can stand on a steady chair and hold it up high.
Time the fall three times each.
Record in the table on ws2.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will be slowest? Will twice as big be twice as slow?'
experiments.why: A bigger canopy has a bigger area pushing against the air. So air resistance grows faster as it falls, and the parachute settles at a slower steady speed.
experiments.safety: An adult does any drop from a height. Never drop from a balcony or lean over a railing.

experiments.title: Shape race in water
experiments.question: Which shape falls fastest through water?
need: a tall clear plastic bottle (1 or 2 litres) full of water
clay or plasticine (atta dough works for a few drops)
a spoon or a long stick to fish shapes out
steps: Make four shapes from equal lumps of clay, each about the size of a big marble: a ball, a flat pancake, a cube and a torpedo (pointed at one end).
Hold two shapes just above the water and let go at the same moment, the torpedo pointed end down.
Watch which one reaches the bottom first.
Race every pair of shapes. Repeat each race three times, swapping hands.
Put the shapes in order from fastest to slowest.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to order the shapes before testing.
experiments.why: Water pushes against the front of anything moving through it. A pointed, smooth shape parts the water a little at a time and leaves less swirling water behind, so there is less water resistance. The flat pancake pushes the most water in front of it, so it falls slowest and often wobbles.

project.title: Balloon rocket
steps: Thread a straw onto a 5 m string and tie the string tight between two chairs.
Blow up a balloon, hold the neck shut, and tape it under the straw. A long balloon works best, but a round one works too.
Let go and measure how far it travels.
Improve it for distance: try a long balloon, a nose cone, less tape, a tighter string. Change one thing at a time.
Draw a force diagram: air pushed backwards, balloon pushed forwards, friction and air resistance holding it back.
Show your best result and explain each improvement.
project.outcome: A balloon rocket, a record of the improvements and a force diagram.

game.title: Force Duel
need: a paper strip as a track with 0 in the middle and 10 each side
rules: Put a coin on 0 of the track (the 'cart').
Shuffle the cards. Deal 5 to each of two players. Player 1 sits at the left end of the track and pushes the cart right. Player 2 sits at the right end and pushes left.
Each turn, both play one card face down, then turn them over together.
Work out the resultant: bigger minus smaller. Move the cart that many spaces towards the smaller player.
Special cards: 'Friction' takes 2 N off the bigger push. 'Balanced!' cancels both pushes this turn. 'Tailwind' adds 3 N to your own push. 'Headwind' takes 3 N off your opponent's push.
After each turn, both players pick up a new card.
First to push the cart off the other player's end wins. Say the resultant aloud each turn.

big: If you threw a ball in deep space, would it ever stop?
Why do racing cyclists and swimmers wear tight, smooth suits?
How can a rocket work in space, where there's no air to push against?
Why don't raindrops hurt, even after falling from a cloud kilometres up?
Can the forces on something be balanced while it's moving fast?

challenge.q: Books often say Faust Vrančić made the first parachute jump, from a tower in Venice in 1617. Is that proven?
challenge.hint: Vrančić published a drawing of a parachute ('Homo Volans', the flying man) in his book Machinae Novae, around 1615. The story of his jump only appears in later accounts, and historians haven't found a reliable record from 1617. The first well-recorded parachute jumps were by Louis-Sébastien Lenormand (1783) and André-Jacques Garnerin (1797). Ask: what would count as good evidence that a jump happened?

challenge.q: 'Balanced forces mean nothing is moving.' True or false?
challenge.hint: A skydiver at a steady speed and a cycle rolling at a steady speed on a flat road both have balanced forces. Balanced means no change in speed or direction, not 'stopped'. Isaac Newton wrote this as his first law of motion, and many adults still get it wrong.

perspectives.view: The rockets of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan had iron cases, which could hold more tightly packed gunpowder than the paper or wooden cases used elsewhere, and they flew further. After the wars, the British engineer William Congreve studied captured rockets and developed his own. Ask: the rocket pushes hot gas backwards. What pushes the rocket forwards?

perspectives.who: A sailor on an uru, the big wooden ship built at Beypore in Kerala
perspectives.view: A sailing ship uses the wind's push on the sail, the water's push on the hull and a rudder to change direction. A good sailor can even sail partly against the wind. Ask: how many forces is the sailor balancing?

perspectives.who: A madar plant on the roadside
perspectives.view: A plant cannot walk, so their seeds must travel away from them to find space to grow. Each madar seed carries a tuft of fine silky hairs. The tuft is very light but spread wide, so air resistance is big and the seed falls slowly, and the wind carries it far. Ask: how is a madar seed like a parachute? Why does a seed with a bigger tuft travel further?

voices.idea: A kingfisher must dive into water without a big splash, which would warn the fish. Their long beak widens slowly towards the head, so it pushes the water aside a little at a time. Japan's first bullet trains had a similar problem: they pushed a wall of air into tunnels, and it burst out of the far end with a loud boom. Eiji Nakatsu, an engineer and a birdwatcher, saw that the train and the kingfisher had the same problem. He redesigned the train's nose to be long and shaped like a kingfisher's beak.
voices.then: Engineers tested many nose shapes in experiments and computer models, and the beak-like shape worked best.
voices.now: The 500 Series Shinkansen (1997) was quieter, faster and used less electricity. Copying nature like this is called biomimicry.
voices.ask: Which Indian animal or bird has a streamlined shape we could copy? What would you design with it?

voices.who: Robert Goddard (1882–1945), USA, and The New York Times
voices.idea: Goddard said rockets could work in space and might one day reach the Moon.
voices.then: In 1920 a New York Times editorial mocked him, saying a rocket couldn't work in space because there was no air for it to push against, and that he seemed to lack the knowledge 'ladled out daily in high schools'.
voices.now: Goddard was right. A rocket pushes its own exhaust gases backwards, and the gases push the rocket forwards. It doesn't need air. On 17 July 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon, the newspaper printed a correction saying it 'regrets the error'.
voices.ask: Our balloon rocket pushed air backwards. In space there's no air outside, but what is still being pushed out of a rocket?

books.title: Gravity
books.author: Jason Chin
books.why: Beautiful, simple, and pairs with this year's gravity topic.

books.title: Who Was Isaac Newton?
books.author: Janet B. Pascal
books.why: The person behind the laws of motion.

books.title: Thing Explainer
books.author: Randall Munroe
books.why: Explains rockets, jet engines and more using only the thousand most common English words. Look at the rocket pages together.

books.title: Wings of Fire
books.author: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam with Arun Tiwari
books.age: Adult book. Read short parts aloud.
books.why: Dr Kalam's own story of India's rocket programme, from the first launch at Thumba in Kerala, which is in this unit's story.

check.a: The overall force when all the forces on something are added up.

check.q: Push 10 N right, friction 3 N left. What happens?
check.a: Resultant 7 N right, so it speeds up to the right.

check.q: What is air resistance, and when is it bigger?
check.a: The push of air against a moving object. It is bigger when the object moves faster or has a bigger front.

check.q: Why does a bigger parachute fall more slowly?
check.a: More area means more air resistance, so it reaches a slower steady speed.

check.q: Can forces be balanced while something moves? Give an example.
check.a: Yes. A cycle at steady speed or a skydiver at terminal speed.

check.q: Why are fish and fast trains pointed at the front?
check.a: Streamlined shapes have less water or air resistance.

check.q: How does a rocket move in space with no air?
check.a: It pushes gas out backwards, and the gas pushes the rocket forwards.

story.title: The Rocket at Thumba
text: In 1963 the fishing village of Thumba, near Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala, got new neighbours. Scientists came to build India's first rocket launching station on the beach, right beside the sea.

Celine was ten. Her family fished from a kattumaram, a boat made of logs tied together. The fishing families who lived near the old church of St Mary Magdalene had agreed to move, and the church and the priest's house were given to the scientists. Where people had once prayed, engineers now bent over wires and tools.
Celine went to watch whenever she could. One morning she saw two young men wheeling a bicycle along the sandy road. Tied to the carrier was a shining metal cone, the pointed tip of a rocket.
"So the air slides past it," one of them said. "A flat nose would have to push the air hard out of the way. That slows the rocket down."

Celine thought about that all day. That evening she asked her uncle, who was mending a net on the sand. "The rocket will go up into the sky, where the air is thin. Then there is nothing there. What will it push against?"

Her uncle shrugged. "When I row, I push the water back with the oar, and the boat goes forward. A crow pushes the air down with their wings. Everything pushes on something. Your rocket will have nothing to push on. Maybe it only works near the ground."
It sounded right. Celine was not sure.

A few days later, she and her little brother Jose took the kattumaram into the shallow water near the shore. Jose stood on the logs, bent his knees and jumped for the sand. He landed on the beach. The kattumaram slid backwards, out into the water, all by itself.

Celine stood very still in the waves. Jose had not pushed on the sand or the water or the air. He had pushed on the boat, and the boat had pushed him back. Two pushes, the same size, in opposite directions. He went one way, and the boat went the other.

On the evening of 21 November 1963, as the sun was going down, the whole village came out onto the beach. The rocket stood on its launcher, thin and white, pointing at the sky. The scientists were very quiet.

Then came a roar, and fire. Hot gas shot down out of the rocket's tail, very hard and very fast, and the rocket climbed. It went slowly at first, then faster and faster, until it was a bright point and then nothing at all. Celine could see that two forces were fighting. The Earth pulled the rocket down. The gas pushed it up. The push was much bigger than the pull, and so the rocket kept speeding up.

Some minutes later, someone shouted and pointed. High above the darkening sea, a glowing orange cloud had appeared. The rocket had let out a puff of a metal called sodium, far up where the sky was still lit by the sun. The scientists were photographing the cloud as it drifted, to see how the winds blow up there, higher than any aeroplane flies.
That night, Jose asked her what the rocket had pushed against, so high where there is almost no air.

"Its own gas," Celine said. "Remember when you jumped off the kattumaram? You pushed the boat back, and the boat pushed you forward. The rocket throws its gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up. It doesn't need the air. It carries the thing it pushes against."
Jose thought about it. "So if I had a big enough boat to throw," he said, "I could fly."
"You would need to throw it very hard, and keep on throwing," said Celine. "That's why the rocket needed all that fire."
The next morning her uncle was on the sand again with his net. Celine sat down beside him and began to explain.
story.epiphany: Every force has a partner force: when one thing pushes another, the second pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction. A rocket does not push on the air. It pushes its exhaust gas down, and the gas pushes it up, so it works where there is no air. While the push from the gas is bigger than the rocket's weight, the forces are unbalanced and the rocket speeds up. The turn is Jose's jump from the kattumaram. The launch at Thumba on 21 November 1963, the church used by the scientists, the rocket parts carried by bicycle and the orange sodium cloud are real. Celine, Jose and their uncle are made up.
ask: Why was the tip of the rocket pointed?
Why did the kattumaram slide backwards when Jose jumped?
What two forces were acting on the rocket as it climbed? Which was bigger?
What did the rocket push against, high up where there is almost no air?
Celine's uncle thought a rocket needs something outside it to push on. Why did that seem sensible?

ideas.idea: Balanced forces mean a steady speed, and a steady speed can be fast.
ideas.more: A cycle rolling on a flat road and a skydiver at top speed both have balanced forces, yet both are moving. Newton's first law: nothing changes its speed or direction unless the forces on it are unbalanced.

ideas.idea: Every force comes in a pair.
ideas.more: Rockets push gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards. You push the Earth down when you jump, and the Earth pushes you up.

ideas.idea: Shape decides how air and water push back.
ideas.more: Pointed, smooth shapes slip through air and water. Wide shapes push a lot of air or water and are slowed. A parachute and a kingfisher's beak use the same physics in opposite ways.

unknowns: Physicists know of four basic forces: gravity, electromagnetism, and two that act inside atoms. How gravity fits together with the other three is the biggest unsolved problem in physics.

Something is making the whole universe spread apart faster and faster. Scientists call it 'dark energy', but nobody knows what it is. It seems to make up about two-thirds of all the energy in the universe.
